title: Development and Quality of Life
summary: What development means, economic and social indicators such as GDP per capita, HDI, literacy and life expectancy, the development gap, and inequality in South Africa.

notes.text: The process of improving people's standard of living and quality of life: their income, health, education, housing, freedom and access to services.

Countries are often grouped as **more economically developed** (high-income), **less economically developed** (low-income) or **developing** (middle-income). South Africa is a middle-income country with great inequality. Another way of describing this is the **North–South divide**: most rich countries are in the northern hemisphere and most poorer ones in the south (with exceptions such as Australia).

notes.caption: Economic and social indicators
rows: The total value of goods and services produced in a year, divided by the population
Average number of years a person can expect to live
Number of babies who die before age 1 per 1 000 live births
Percentage of adults who can read and write
Access to clean water and sanitation
Percentage of people with safe water and toilets

notes.title: Calculating GDP per capita
notes.problem: A country has a GDP of R6 000 billion and a population of 60 million. Calculate the GDP per capita.

notes.text: A measure created by the United Nations that combines three things: **life expectancy** (health), **years of schooling** (education) and **income per person** (standard of living). It ranges from 0 to 1; the closer to 1, the more developed.

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: GDP per capita is only an **average**. It does not show how wealth is shared. A country can have a high GDP per capita while many people remain poor.

notes.title: Comparing two countries
notes.problem: Country A: life expectancy 58, adult literacy 70%. Country B: life expectancy 79, adult literacy 98%. Which is more developed, and why are several indicators better than one?
steps: Higher life expectancy points to better health care and nutrition, favouring B.
Higher literacy points to better education, favouring B.
One figure can mislead: income alone does not show health or education.
notes.answer: Country B, as both indicators are higher.

notes.text: South Africa is one of the most **unequal** countries in the world, measured by the **Gini coefficient** (0 = perfect equality, 1 = one person has everything); South Africa's is about 0,63. Inequality exists between rich and poor, between urban and rural areas, between provinces (Gauteng and the Western Cape are wealthier than Limpopo and the Eastern Cape), and still largely along racial lines because of apartheid.
Why are some places less developed?

items: **History**: colonialism and apartheid took resources and denied people education and land.
**Trade**: exporting low-value raw materials and importing expensive manufactured goods.
**Debt**: poor countries spend money on repaying loans instead of services.
**Natural factors**: drought, floods, poor soil, disease (malaria, HIV).
**Governance**: corruption and conflict waste resources and scare away investors.
**Lack of infrastructure**: roads, electricity and water are needed for businesses to grow.
